extracted.intended_audience: piano teachers, serious piano students, and professional pianists
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and interpretive guidance for piano teaching, practice, and performance drawn from interviews with established pianists and teachers; covers pedagogy, touch, interpretation, memorization, repertoire maintenance, and technical study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher's work should speak for itself
rubrics_metrics.description: A teacher's value is shown by the success of pupils rather than advertising or claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author claims he 'never advertise[s]' and can 'point to hundreds of pupils... who are constantly before the public' as proof of effectiveness. Implication: tangible pupil achievements are the principal credential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how to improve (diagnosis + remedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers must not merely tell pupils they play badly; they must explain how to play better, identify causes of faults, and provide corrective instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of teachers who 'say to the pupil:

rubrics_metrics.name: Matthay's lesson method
rubrics_metrics.description: Listen to a complete performance, then go back and work through the piece for corrections and suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matthay 'listens to a complete performance of the work in hand, then turns back to the beginning and goes over it again for corrections and suggestions.' He uses physical gestures (dashes down chord, lays restraining hand), adds phrasing marks with a blue pencil, and discusses character and intended effects. Also exemplified by the motto: 'Never touch the piano without trying to make music.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven focal points of musical interpretation (from Musical Interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected seven themes for elucidation in teaching and performing: 1) difference between Practise and Strumming; 2) difference between Teaching and Cramming; 3) how one's mind can be brought to bear on one's work; 4) correct ideas of Time and Shape; 5) elements of Rubato and its application; 6) elements of Duration and Pedaling and their application; 7) details as to the application of the Element of Tone-variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These seven points form the book's organizing rubric; several are elaborated elsewhere on the page (rubato, pedaling, tone-variety, time/shape, mental focus, practice quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubato: bending not breaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubato is the bending of time, not breaking it; extra time given to certain notes must be taken from others to even things up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author warns inexperienced players often 'think that rubato means breaking the time.' Illustrated with examples from compositions to show correct application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedaling: avoid misuse of damper pedal
rubrics_metrics.description: Damper pedal misuse can ruin phrasing and tonal effects produced by the fingers; pedaling should be carefully applied in relation to sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedaling is 'aptly explained by means of numerous illustrations.' Faults often traced to inattention to the sounds produced; pedagogy should emphasize listening to the instrument when using pedal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone-variety: beauty arises from relations between tones
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single beautiful piano tone in isolation; beauty on piano results from the relation and variety between successive tones and contrasts of intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare singer/violinist (can color a single tone) to pianist (must use succession and contrast). A harsh note can be beautiful 'if in the right place' because of its expressive meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-emphasis on external technic at expense of musical ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical externals (hand shape, perfectly even scales) are less important than achieving musical effects; much time is wasted on externals that do not reach the heart of the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bauer's account: he initially sought effects quickly without concern for how the hand looked; later refined externals when time allowed. Warning against 'long, laborious' methods that miss vital points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scales should not be perfectly even; cultivate variety
rubrics_metrics.description: A scale should have rhythmic and tonal variations; an absolutely even scale is 'monotonous' and 'poisonous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bauer demonstrates that both the untrained blurred scale and the mechanically even 'correct' scale are undesirable; the goal is lively variety, not machine-like regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: prioritize expression and thought over mechanical uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation requires tonal and rhythmic modification across many subtle shades; personal expression and daily variability are natural and desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four crude divisions of expression: loud, soft, fast, slow—within which 'infinite shades and gradations' exist. Avoid binding oneself to a fixed rendition; humans naturally vary between performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study a new composition from the musical side first
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the meaning, ideas, and overall conception of a piece before working on technical execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bauer compares to painters who worked out color studies before finished drawings; the 'art thought' should precede technical detail when learning a new piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tempo/velocity should serve the musical spirit, not rigid rules
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no absolute rule for tempo; velocity is part of thought and cultural inclination and must be chosen to project the meaning and spirit of the composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Velocity can be inherent; different people conceive of 'fast' differently. The important test is whether the performer can make the piece's meaning alive to listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power derives from contrast rather than brute strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient power is achieved through contrast and placement; it's not merely exertion of great muscular force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasional pounding is acceptable, but overall power comes from contrast and the player's understanding of content to place effects in 'right time and place.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Training young children: health, ear, and basics first
rubrics_metrics.description: Children may begin at five or six if robust; emphasize physical health, ear training (tone discrimination, solfeggio), proper hand position, and thorough drill in scales, arpeggios, chords, and finger exercises before pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early training should include etudes (Czerny, Cramer, Clementi) and Bach; avoid overworking and take care of child's health to prevent overdoing study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pugno's focus: inner meaning over technical drills
rubrics_metrics.description: Pugno concerned himself mainly with translating themes into feelings and discussing interpretation rather than technical instruction; technical faults could lead him to stop the lesson until corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He would 'close the music book and refuse to listen' if technical faults persisted. He often played along or sang to give pupils ideas of meaning, fostering independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of touch: Melody Hand vs Technical/Coloratura Hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Different touch/hand positions are required depending on whether one wants lyrical, full tone (Melody Hand) or rapid, articulate passage work (Technical/Coloratura Hand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melody Hand: outstretched, flat fingers, weighty/relaxed, 'caressing' pressure. Technical Hand: arched, rounded fingers, fingers' tips on keys, quick finger action, 'alive' hand. The two can be blended and modified as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three melody touches: down, up, wiping-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody playing uses three specific touches—down touch (descending arm), up touch (elevating the wrist while finger lies on key), and wiping-off touch (drawing finger off key with arm/hand movement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach melody touch starting with single-tone exercises and apply to lyric pieces (e.g., Mendelssohn's Songs without Words) to internalize the effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical touch details (coloratura technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: For rapid, brilliant passage work use arched hand, well-rounded fingers whose tips fall cleanly on keys; fingers should 'fall' rather than strike and maintain even, clean lifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical hand posture and finger action should be practiced so player can produce clear, articulate, 'sparkling' passage work without hitting or striking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assimilation of principles: make touch automatic and situational
rubrics_metrics.description: Pianists should learn and assimilate touch principles so that on seeing a passage they immediately know the touch required to express it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to trained actors whose features automatically assume necessary expression; thorough training places various touches 'at one's finger-tips' allowing natural expressive response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorization: know the music away from the piano and be able to resume from corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorize every note away from the instrument and be able to continue from any corrected measure without restarting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some students naturally memorize away from the piano; teacher accepts different successful methods but requires thoroughness so corrections can be integrated seamlessly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Octave study method ('octave grimace' and progressive endurance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the hand with arched position and slightly curved unemployed fingers ('octave grimace'); practice starting with one beat in 16ths, ending with wiping-off touch, progressively increasing duration and chromatic coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be played full keyboard in all keys and chromatically; build up to prolonged playing (twenty minutes) so octave passages become manageable without exhaustive repetitive practice of the piece itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping repertoire in repair: systematic weekly rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize repertoire into groups and rotate weekly so each composer/genre is reviewed; identify weak places and practice those specifically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example schedule: Monday Chopin (play whole list, then fix weak spots), Tuesday Schumann, then Liszt, Russian, modern composers, concertos, chamber music—systematic maintenance keeps repertoire 'in repair.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice details: daily structure and focused technical study
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedicate mornings to practice (at least one hour to technic: scales, arpeggios, octaves, chords, Bach) and afternoons to teaching; prefer perfecting a few etudes/Bach pieces thoroughly rather than many superficially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work one Bach invention in various ways (transposing, polishing), and bring a few etudes up to the highest degree of completeness instead of attempting many half-learned pieces.
